# Example 3 (Intermediate) {.unnumbered}

This example illustrates the usage of the evaluate endpoint and inline model manipulations. It builds a simple pickup/dropoff (similar to the basic model) and runs an eval on a sub-sequence to illustrate how to call the endpoint and interpret the responses in terms of infeasibility messages.

## Data 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

data <- read.csv('../../../sample_data/publist_orders.csv')

number_pubs <- nrow(data)
```

The data used in this example is a list of `r number_pubs` pubs in Dublin, Ireland with their associated X and Y coordinates and quantities (amount added to a vehicle at each location).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false

if(!("pacman" %in% rownames(installed.packages()))){
  install.packages("pacman")
}

library(pacman)
p_load(tidyverse)
p_load(DT)
p_load(dplyr)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

data <- data %>% select(-c(pickupTime,dropoffTime)) %>% mutate(across(2:3, ~ format(round(.x, digits=5), nsmall = 5))) 

datatable(data, colnames = c("Pub Name (id)",
                           "X-Coordinate (X)",
                           "Y-Coordinate (Y)",
                           "Quantity (quantity)")
                           , options = list(dom = 't', scrollY = "200px", pageLength=nrow(data), columnDefs = list(list(className = 'dt-right', targets = 2:4))))
```

## Running the example

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
library(iceR)

source('ivr7-model-helper.R')
```

Execute the example as follows:

### 1. Create an apiHelper object with the model type you'd like to solve

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
api <- new("apiHelper", modelType = 'ivr7-kt461v8eoaif', configFile = '../../../config.json')
```

### 2. Create the model and add some data to it

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Create the model
sr <- new (IVR7.SolveRequest)
sr$model <- new (IVR7.Model)

# Load the data
data <- read.csv('../../../sample_data/publist_orders.csv')

# Configure the model and add the data to it (See ivr7-model-helper.R for details around some of the methods used below)
sr$model$dimensions <- make_distance_time_cap_dims()
sr$model$locations <- make_locations(data)
sr$model$jobs <- make_job_time_cap(data, src = rep(1, nrow(data) - 1), dest = 2:nrow(data))
sr$model$vehicleCostClasses <- make_vcc_simple('vcc1', 1000, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 1, 3)
sr$model$vehicleClasses <- make_vc_simple('vc1', 1, 1, 1, 1)
sr$model$vehicles <- lapply(1:4, function(i){
  make_vehicle_cap( paste0("vehicle_", i), 'vc1', 'vcc1',
                    2000, # the vehicle capacity
                    data$id[1], # start location
                    data$id[1], # end location
                    7*60,  # 7 AM
                    18*60) # 6 PM
})

# Set the other relevant information
sr$solveType <- 0 # 0 for optimise, 1 for evaluate, 2 for reoptimise

# View the model in plain-text format (string or JSON)
sr$model$toString() %>% cat
sr$model$toJSON() %>% cat
```

### 3. Submit the model to the API

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
requestID <- api %>% postSolveRequest(sr)  
```

### 4. Retrieve the model response

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
resp <- api %>% getResponse(requestID)
```

### 5. Look at the result

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Get the solve time
solveTime <- api %>% getSolveTime(requestID)
```

Solve time: `r solveTime`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Tabulate the data in native-R format
tab <- resp %>% tabulate(sr)
tab$nodes %>% head # just inspect the head of the output
tab$edges %>% head # just inspect the head of the output


# Plot the data (ggplot or leaflet)
resp %>% plotResponse(sr) # ggplot                       
resp %>% plotResponseLeaflet(sr) # leaflet (if it's mappable)
```

## Manipulating the model and evaluating

At this point it may be interesting to see the effect of adding constraints which weren't in the original model.

**Step 1**: Add time windows and convert to a task sequence

 We can add some time windows (08:00-14:00) to all the locations. In order to evaluate our current solution against this new solution, we need to convert our current solution to a task sequence (which is done by vehicle - list the tasks that each vehicle should perform; each item in the list is another vehicle; vehicles with no tasks can be omitted).

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# (a) Add time windows
for(i in 1:length(sr$model$locations)){
  la <- new (IVR7.Location.Attribute)
  la$dimensionId <- 'time'
  la$quantity <- 0
  w <- new (IVR7.Window)
  w$start <- 8*60 # 08:00 in our world, because we're measuring in minutes
  w$end <- 14*60  # 14:00
  la$arrivalWindows <- w  # Adding this as an arrival window. We could also add it as a departure window
  sr$model$locations[[i]]$attributes <- la
}        

# (b) Convert the current solution to a task sequence
# The only catch here is that the shift-start and shift-end nodes are implicitly 
# already there so all we really need to do is pull out the nodes inbetween. 
# So we filter on only the tasks we're scheduling in the last solution we received.
sr$model$taskSequence <- list()
vs <- tab$nodes$vehicleId %>% unique() # the unique set of vehicles in the solution
for(v in vs){
  ts <- new (IVR7.TaskSequence)
  ts$vehicleId <- v
  ts$taskId <-  tab$nodes %>%
    filter(grepl(x = taskId, pattern = 'pickup_') |
             grepl(x = taskId, pattern = 'dropoff_'),
           vehicleId == v) %>%
    select(taskId) %>% unlist %>% as.character()
  sr$model$taskSequence[[length(sr$model$taskSequence) + 1]] <- ts
}

sr$model$taskSequence[[1]]$toString() %>% cat

# Set the other relevant information (in this case, tell the solver to use the evaluation solve process)
sr$solveType <- 1 # 0 for optimise, 1 for evaluate, 2 for reoptimise

# Submit the model to the API
requestID <- api %>% postSolveRequest(sr)  

# Retrieve the model response
evalresp <- api %>% getResponse(requestID)  
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Look at the result
tabeval <- evalresp %>% tabulate(sr)
tabeval$infeasibilities %>% head
```
Here we see that we have some constraints which have been broken. We get told which dimension is related (if the constraint is related to a dimension), the type of constraint (if known) and the degree to which the constraint is broken.

If the constraints are tardy constraints being broken, this means the task starts AFTER the allowable window. The limit will often be zero and the value will be the amount by which the vehicle is late. 

We can check the arrival time of the task to verify this. We know that we set all the location windows to be between 08:00 and 14:00. Filter on all tasks which appear in the infeasibility set and let's check their windows.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

tabeval$nodes %>% filter(taskId %in% tabeval$infeasibilities$taskId) %>%
  select(time_start) %>% mutate(windowBroken = time_start > 14*60)
```

All the tasks flagged by the infeasibilities table correspond to tasks in the schedule which will arrive after the permissable window.

**Step 2**: Take out all infeasible tasks

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

for(i in 1:length(sr$model$taskSequence)){
  ts <- sr$model$taskSequence[[i]]$taskId
  sr$model$taskSequence[[i]]$taskId <- ts[!(ts %in% tabeval$infeasibilities$taskId)]
  # just remove any tasks seen in the tabeval$infeasibilities set
}       
```
The pickups were mostly feasible on their time windows, it was just the dropoffs that were a problem. What will happen when we have pickups without dropoffs?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Submit the model to the API
requestID <- api %>% postSolveRequest(sr)  

# Retrieve the model response
evalresp <- api %>% getResponse(requestID)  
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Look at the result
tabeval <- evalresp %>% tabulate(sr)
tabeval$infeasibilities %>% head
```

We find that there are a whole bunch of precendence constraints (cumul-pair constraints and task-pair constraints) which are then broken. This is because there's a relation between the pickup and dropoff and either they're BOTH scheduled or BOTH unscheduled. Having one task assigned to a vehicle in the schedule without the other breaks a bunch of constraints. We need to remove these stops.

**Step 3**: Take out all infeasible tasks (again)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

for(i in 1:length(sr$model$taskSequence)){
  ts <- sr$model$taskSequence[[i]]$taskId
  sr$model$taskSequence[[i]]$taskId <- ts[!(ts %in% tabeval$infeasibilities$taskId)]
  # just remove any tasks seen in the tabeval$infeasibilities set
}    

# Submit the model to the API
requestID <- api %>% postSolveRequest(sr)  

# Retrieve the model response
evalresp <- api %>% getResponse(requestID)  
```
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Look at the result
tabeval <- evalresp %>% tabulate(sr)
tabeval$infeasibilities %>% head
```

This is now NULL, which means there aren't any infeasibilities left in the schedule. However, at what cost did this come?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

if( !(evalresp$objective > resp$objective) ){
  stop("Only true if the cost of dropping a job is close to zero.")
}
```

It is evident the new schedule costs more (because a bunch of jobs have been left off). 

NOTE: The evaluate still comes back with all the same things as before, so plotting is identical and the interpretation of the schedule is also the same. The only thing is that it will permit infeasible actions but then report on where constraints are being broken (such as slack (earlyness), tardiness (lateness)), precedence, capacity and task/location windows.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Plot the data (leaflet)
evalresp %>%  plotResponseLeaflet(sr) 
# This is just the feasible subset with the evaluate endpoint.
```

We can switch back to an optimise request. Drop the task sequence and let the optimiser do its thing with the new window constraints.

### Running the request (with the added time windows)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

# Drop the task sequence
sr$model$taskSequence <- list()

# Set the other relevant information (switch back to the optimise option)
sr$solveType <- 1 # 0 for optimise, 1 for evaluate, 2 for reoptimise

# Submit the model to the API
requestID <- api %>% postSolveRequest(sr)  

# Retrieve the model response
window_constrained_resp <- api %>% getResponse(requestID)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# Look at the result
wtab <- window_constrained_resp %>% tabulate(sr)

window_constrained_resp$objective > resp$objective 
# We expect the new solution to cost more because of the additional constraints
window_constrained_resp$infeasibilities            
# There won't be any infeasibilities because the request was to # "optimise" not "evaluate" and this problem instance is largely unconstrained 
# (i.e. it's easy for the solver to find a way to satisfy all the tasks)
```
